Abstract
NeuroCare AI is a university software and machine-learning project that demonstrates classification of a diabetes-related
label in a historical public health survey. It connects a React/TypeScript interface, a FastAPI service, a TensorFlow/Keras
artificial neural network (ANN), and PostgreSQL persistence. Users enter a fictional profile containing 21 coded survey
features, review their answers, and receive the model's class, score, version and decision threshold after a database save.
The application is an educational prototype, not a diagnostic, screening or individual future-risk tool.
The configured model uses a processed cohort of 222,600 BRFSS 2021 records. Its ANN has two hidden dense layers of 64
and 32 units and a sigmoid output. On 40,376 previously evaluated test records, the model achieves 67.04% accuracy,
29.78% precision, 82.82% recall and ROC AUC 0.8129. F1, calculated for this report from the saved confusion matrix, is
0.4381. These results indicate useful ranking of survey labels within this cohort but substantial classification errors: 1,076
positive labels are missed and 12,231 negative labels are flagged positive. They do not establish clinical validity or reliable
performance in another population.
The documentation exercise reran 127 selected backend tests and 27 frontend tests, lint, type checking, the production
build and an independent model-integrity audit. Three selected HTTP tests were deselected; the complete backend suite
and database-writing integration tests were not run. A read-only database probe could not complete in this execution
context. Earlier browser verification is identified separately from checks executed for this report. Application source,
model, database records and configuration were not changed to produce this documentation.
1. Introduction and objectives
1.1 Purpose and problem addressed
An isolated trained model does not demonstrate how a complete machine-learning application works. Inputs must have
consistent meanings, validation must reject invalid values, the same preprocessing must be used in training and inference,
and stored results must identify the model that produced them. NeuroCare addresses these engineering requirements
through an inspectable educational application.
The documented objective is to connect a real ANN with a working interface and persistent backend while explaining the
evidence and limitations. Its subject is classification of a survey label, not diagnosis from clinical measurements. Although
API and interface terminology includes “prediction,” the implementation does not estimate the probability of future
diabetes or establish an individual's health status.
1.2 Specific objectives
The implemented objectives are to expose the exact 21-feature contract; preserve source category meanings; demonstrate
offline model preparation and training; serve a versioned model without retraining per request; validate submissions on
both client and server; store successful outputs transactionally; and present evaluation alongside limitations. The website
also makes architecture, dataset provenance and educational-use guidance visible.

3. System architecture
3.1 Separation of responsibilities
The browser handles presentation, temporary form state and client validation. FastAPI provides the public contract and
validates requests. A service coordinates inference and persistence. A repository commits prediction rows through
SQLAlchemy/Psycopg. The predictor loads a trusted local Keras artifact and saved preprocessing. Offline training is
separate from HTTP inference.

System architecture. Offline training supplies trusted artifacts; online inference and transactional persistence have separate
responsibilities.
The dependency direction supports independent testing: service tests can use controlled predictor/session doubles, while
artifact tests load the actual model. These test types prove different things; simulated sessions do not prove a live
PostgreSQL save.
3.2 Important boundaries
The inference path does not call training. Keras loads with compilation disabled and safe_mode=True, and inference uses
training=False. Saved feature order is enforced independently of JSON key order. Configuration and predictor objects are
cached within a process, so changing a model directory requires an API restart to replace cached state.
The database is not replaced by browser storage or a local JSON file. Successful responses follow a database commit, while
unavailable services produce explicit errors. Public business endpoints expose model information and submission, not a
history listing.
3.3 Development startup
The documented root command is:
.\scripts\dev.ps1 start
The launcher checks existing application listeners, reuses healthy project services, checks PostgreSQL readiness, applies
migrations and starts only missing API/frontend processes. It records process ownership so cleanup stops only the
application processes it started. PostgreSQL on 5432 is independently managed; helper guards refuse to launch, rebind or
stop a project cluster on that port. This behavior was inspected in source, not re-executed during the documentation run
because startup may apply migrations.
See architecture.md for component boundaries and a transaction sequence.

4.4 Missing values and validation
Only explicitly supported raw codes are mapped. Unknown/refused responses remain missing and are excluded by
complete-case filtering. Code 88 becomes zero only for the mental/physical health-day fields. BMI's two implied decimal
places are restored, then rounded to an integer using ties-to-even rounding; out-of-range values are excluded rather than
clipped.
The processed CSV must contain exactly the target and 21 named features. Each value is checked for numeric finiteness,
integer coding and allowed range. These checks prevent malformed source files from silently changing the inference
contract. They do not remove self-report error or selection bias.
4.5 Splitting and cross-year overlap protection
An earlier 2015 dataset and model were used for development and transfer initialization. The 2021 workflow does not
simply concatenate both years. It removes profiles matching earlier held-out profiles and forces 20,789 matches to prior
training profiles into training only. Novel profiles are divided with five shuffled, stratified group folds and seed 42. Identical
feature profiles remain in one partition, even if their labels differ. Group stratification aims to preserve label balance
subject to the grouping constraint. [R8]

6.5 Overfitting, generalization and leakage
Overfitting occurs when learned patterns or development decisions fit available development data better than genuinely
new examples. Dropout, L2 and validation-loss early stopping address some model-fitting risks. They do not correct
self-report bias or make repeated test-set reuse independent.
Generalization means performance beyond the training/development records. The project has no verified prospective,
independent clinical evaluation, current-population calibration or subgroup fairness study. No claim of suitability for
another country, time period or healthcare setting follows from the reported metrics.
Data leakage is unintended use of held-out information in training or selection. Training-only normalization, grouped
partitions and cross-year quarantine reduce identifiable leakage paths. They cannot verify participant identity, prove
absence of every leakage mechanism, or undo the effects of repeated human evaluation of the same test set. Brier score
alone does not establish calibration; no reliability diagram or subgroup calibration audit is provided.
7. End-to-end workflow
1. The browser opens a public route and loads the input contract and model metadata. Missing information produces a
loading/unavailable state rather than substitute predictions or metrics.
2. The user creates a fictional profile through Background, Health, Daily life and Wellbeing groups. Values remain in React
state; zero is preserved as a valid answer.
3. Client validation checks presence, integer values and source bounds. The user reviews all 21 answers and may edit
earlier groups without losing other answers.
4. On submission, Axios sends JSON to POST /api/v1/predictions. A submission lock prevents concurrent duplicate clicks,
and requests are not automatically retried.
5. FastAPI/Pydantic rejects missing/extra fields, wrong types and out-of-range values with a sanitized 422 response.
6. The predictor validates the configured artifact/serving contract, orders inputs by FEATURES, applies saved training
statistics, and evaluates the ANN with dropout disabled.
7. The sigmoid score is compared with the saved threshold to generate class 0 or 1.
8. The repository adds a prediction row, commits and refreshes it. On failure it rolls back and raises an error; there is no
success response claiming an unsaved result.
9. A 201 response returns the record ID, class, score, model version, threshold and educational/policy notice. The
interface displays these actual values and moves focus to the result heading.
10. “Try another profile” clears browser form state. It does not delete the stored row or expose anyone else's history.
A network timeout may occur after a successful commit, so a lost response does not prove that no row was saved. The
frontend explains this uncertainty. There is no server-side idempotency-key implementation; a manual repeat could create

12. Strengths, weaknesses and limitations
12.1 Strengths
The project demonstrates a complete frontend/API/model/database integration rather than a disconnected notebook. A
common field definition reduces form/server drift. Offline training, training-only preprocessing and versioned inference
support reproducibility. Transactional persistence and explicit failure states avoid simulated success. The interface exposes
real evaluation, source meanings and limitations, and the code includes simpler-model and majority baselines.
Grouping identical profiles and quarantining historical held-out matches are more careful than a naive random row split.
The audit independently checks important integrity claims. Selected regression tests cover both ordinary behavior and
failure cases, while the launcher is designed to reuse the existing PostgreSQL service and avoid unrelated process cleanup.
12.2 Principal limitations
The current operating point still misses approximately 17% of positive survey labels and produces many false alarms.
Precision is about 30%. Overall accuracy is lower than an all-negative baseline because the policy prioritizes positive
detection; that tradeoff may be instructive, but does not establish real-world utility.
Complete-case exclusion of nearly half the source wave, self-reporting, coarse/combined categories, lack of survey weights
and changed questions limit representativeness. The retained cohort is not a weighted estimate of the general population.
Grouping by profile is not grouping by verified participant. Cross-year source/target comparability is incomplete.
Repeated use of the development test partition prevents treating the current report as new independent validation.
Fairness across age, sex, income or other groups has not been evaluated. Calibration, prospective usefulness, clinical error
costs and external-population performance remain unverified. The broad configured database login and absent
security/governance features constrain deployment beyond a local fictional-data exercise.

the transparent integration and the illustration of why classification thresholds and class imbalance must be considered
alongside headline accuracy.
